You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader. Write Markdown only, never HTML.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Add nothing to a fact: no benefit, cause, consequence or comparison it does not state itself, however likely it seems. If a fact says the strainer has two ears, do not write that the ears rest on the mug's rim; if a fact says a tin holds 100 g of tea, do not write that a 60 g bag fits in it; if a fact says the grinder has 30 settings, do not write that this makes it easy to dial in. State the fact plainly, and put any general advice in its own sentence that does not name the product.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Reuse Candle Jars: Cleaning Tips and Second-Life Ideas
Meta description: Learn how to get leftover wax out of a finished candle jar, clean it and remove the label, plus easy ideas for giving your empty jar a second life.
Slug: how-to-reuse-candle-jars

To reuse a candle jar, let it cool completely, get the leftover wax out (freezing it or using hot water both work well), pry off the metal wick tab, then wash the jar in warm soapy water and peel away any label. After that it's ready for a new job: holding pens, cotton swabs, spices, a little succulent or even a fresh batch of homemade candle wax. Below, we walk through each step and share which Tidewell vessels are especially worth keeping once the candle is done.

## When a Candle Is Really Done

A good rule of thumb is to stop burning a container candle when about half an inch of wax is left in the bottom [G]. Burning all the way down puts the flame right next to the base of the container, which can overheat the glass or ceramic and, in the worst case, cause it to crack. That last layer of wax is your safety cushion, so when you reach it, it's time to say goodbye to the candle and hello to a new jar.

Once you've blown out the flame for the last time, give the container plenty of time to cool all the way through. Don't rush it into the freezer or under cold water while it's still warm, because sudden temperature changes can stress glass and ceramic. Patience here keeps your jar in one piece.

## Getting the Leftover Wax Out

There are a few easy ways to clear out the remaining wax. Pick whichever suits your jar and your kitchen.

### The freezer method

This is the least messy option. Pop the cooled jar into the freezer for a few hours or overnight. As the wax gets cold it shrinks and pulls away from the sides, so you can usually pop it out in one piece with a butter knife or spoon. It works best with jars that have a wide opening.

### The hot-water method

Set the jar on a folded towel in the sink and fill it with hot water, leaving a little room at the top. The heat softens and melts the wax, which floats to the surface. Let the water cool, and the wax will firm up into a disc you can simply lift off. Start with hot tap water rather than boiling water if your container is thin, and never pour melted wax down the drain, since it can harden in the pipes.

### Warm and pour

For a bigger amount of leftover wax, stand the jar in a pan of gently simmering water, like a double boiler. Once the wax has softened to liquid, carefully pour it into a paper-lined container or an old tin to throw away (or save it for wax melts). Wipe out the thin layer that's left with a paper towel while it's still soft.

### Why soy and coconut-soy wax make life easier

Softer natural waxes like soy and coconut-soy blends tend to release from a container more easily than harder waxes, and any film left behind usually washes up with warm soapy water. Our [Sea Salt Soy Candle](P1) is made of 100% soy wax [F2]. Our [Cedar Wood-Wick Candle](P2) is made with a coconut and soy wax blend [F13].

### Removing the wick tab

At the bottom of most container candles sits a small metal tab that held the wick in place. Once the wax is out, slide a butter knife underneath and gently lever it up. If a sticky adhesive dot stays behind, a little cooking oil on a paper towel will loosen it.

## Cleaning and Removing Labels

With the wax gone, it's time to make your jar sparkle.

- **Wash it well.** Use warm soapy water and a sponge or bottle brush to remove any remaining wax film and soot. A second rinse in hot water helps if the inside still feels slightly greasy.
- **Soak off the label.** Most paper labels come off after a soak in warm water. Peel slowly from one corner.
- **Tackle sticky residue.** Rub leftover adhesive with a little cooking oil, or make a paste of baking soda and oil, let it sit for a few minutes, then scrub it away. Rubbing alcohol also works on stubborn spots.
- **Dry thoroughly.** Let the jar air-dry completely, especially if you plan to store dry goods like tea or spices in it.

### Glass versus ceramic

Glass is easy to work with: a non-scratch sponge and some elbow grease handle most residue, and you can hold it up to the light to check for any lingering wax film. Ceramic needs a slightly gentler touch. Glazed surfaces wipe clean easily, but unglazed areas (often the base) can soak up oil, so stick to soap and water there rather than oily residue removers. Unless the maker says otherwise, hand washing is the kindest choice for both.

## Ideas for Your Empty Jar

Once it's clean, your jar can take on all kinds of new roles around the house:

- **Bathroom storage:** cotton swabs, cotton pads, hair ties or bobby pins.
- **Pen or brush holder:** a tidy home for pens on your desk or makeup brushes on your vanity.
- **Small planter:** perfect for a succulent or a little herb. Add a layer of pebbles at the bottom for drainage, since most candle containers don't have holes.
- **Pantry jar:** loose-leaf tea, spices, sugar cubes or snacks.
- **Mini vase:** a few small stems, a sprig of eucalyptus or wildflowers from the garden.
- **Homemade candle:** refill it with new wax and a fresh wick for a DIY candle in a container you already love.
- **Odds and ends:** matches, paper clips, keys or spare buttons.

## Tidewell Jars Worth Keeping

Some containers are just too nice to recycle, and two in our range are made to stick around.

The Sea Salt Soy Candle comes in an 8 oz amber glass jar [F7]. Its jar has a tin lid [F8]. A lidded container is handy for anything you want to keep covered, like loose-leaf tea, bath salts or cotton pads, and amber glass looks lovely on a bathroom shelf or pantry counter.

{{P1}}

The Cedar Wood-Wick Candle comes in a 12 oz ceramic vessel [F16]. Its vessel is reusable [F17]. A sturdy ceramic container makes a natural planter for a small succulent or a desk cup for pens and pencils.

{{P2}}

## Enjoying the Candle Before the Jar

Of course, the best part comes first: enjoying every hour of the candle itself.

- **Sea Salt Soy Candle:** It is poured by hand in Portland, Maine [F3]. It has scent notes of sea salt, driftwood and sage [F9]. It has a cotton wick that is lead-free [F4, F5]. Its burn time is about 45 hours [F6].
- **Cedar Wood-Wick Candle:** It has a cherry-wood wick that crackles as it burns [F14]. It has scent notes of cedar, black pepper and vetiver [F19]. Its burn time is about 60 hours [F15]. Its wick should be trimmed to 3 mm before each burn [F18].

Whichever you choose, burn it with care, stop when that last layer of wax remains, and you'll end up with a lovely jar ready for its second life. When you're ready for your next candle, browse our full [candle collection](L1).
</draft>

<problems>
1. review, grounding 2/5: Most product sentences match their cited facts. However, the article says both Tidewell containers are 'made to stick around'. Only the Cedar vessel is stated to be reusable (F17); nothing says the Sea Salt jar was designed for reuse. The soy section also implies Tidewell candles release from the jar easily, which no fact supports.
2. "Some containers are just too nice to recycle, and two in our range are made to stick around." — Claims both containers are made for reuse. Only the Cedar Wood-Wick vessel is stated as reusable (F17); no fact says the Sea Salt Soy jar was designed to be kept.
3. "Below, we walk through each step and share which Tidewell vessels are especially worth keeping once the candle is done." — Frames Tidewell vessels as especially reuse-worthy, which goes beyond the facts for P1.
4. "Softer natural waxes like soy and coconut-soy blends tend to release from a container more easily than harder waxes, and any film left behind usually washes up with warm soapy water." — This sentence is unmarked, and it sits directly before the product citations. Together they imply Tidewell candles clean out easily, a property the facts do not state.
5. "Its wick should be trimmed to 3 mm before each burn [F18]." — The whole 'Enjoying the Candle Before the Jar' section lists product features unrelated to reusing jars. It reads as a sales pitch and is off topic.
</problems>
